group.passage: Long before GPS, sailors approaching a rocky coast at night had to trust a light on the shore. The earliest of these lights were simply fires burning on raised platforms. The most famous early tower, the Pharos of Alexandria in Egypt, was completed in the third century BC and kept a fire burning at its top. It became so well known that its name turned into the Greek word for “lighthouse.” For many centuries, however, the light itself stayed weak. Keepers burned wood and coal, then moved on to candles and to lamps fueled by whale oil, animal fat, and later kerosene. An open flame wastes almost all of its glow: nearly 97 percent of the light is lost. Mirrors placed behind the flame helped, but even the brightest beams could be seen only 8 to 12 miles away. The breakthrough came in 1822, when a scientist named Augustin Fresnel introduced a new kind of lens, first placed in a lighthouse in France. Instead of one thick piece of glass, it used hundreds of carefully cut prisms that bent scattered rays into a single strong beam. A Fresnel lens lost no more than 20 percent of the light, and the largest ones could be seen more than 20 miles out at sea. Because the lens could turn, each lighthouse could also flash its own pattern, so sailors could tell one light from another. These brighter lights still depended on people. Keepers lit the lamp at sunset and put it out at sunrise, climbed the tower at night to wind the clockwork that turned the lens, and polished the glass for hours. One of their chores, cutting the burning wick so that it would not smoke and dirty the lens, earned them the nickname “wickies.” Electricity began to change all of this. American lighthouses started switching to electric power in 1900, slowly at first and then rapidly in the 1920s and 1930s. With fewer tasks left, fewer keepers were needed, and in the mid-1960s the United States began a program to automate its lights. By 1990, every American lighthouse except Boston Light ran without a keeper. Today, as GPS makes them far less important, many old towers survive as museums or even as places to spend the night.

translation_zh.text:
早在 GPS 出現之前，夜裡駛近岩岸的水手只能信賴岸上的一盞燈。最早的這種燈，不過是在高臺上燃燒的火堆。早期最有名的燈塔是埃及的亞歷山卓燈塔（Pharos），在西元前三世紀完工，塔頂一直燃著火。它名氣大到連名字都變成了希臘文的「燈塔」一詞。

然而，好幾個世紀以來，燈光本身一直很微弱。守塔人燒過木柴和煤，後來改用蠟燭，以及燒鯨油、動物油脂、再後來是煤油的油燈。開放的火焰幾乎浪費了所有的光：將近 97% 的光都散失了。在火焰後方放鏡子有些幫助，但即使是最亮的光束，也只能在 8 到 12 英里外看見。

突破出現在 1822 年。一位名叫奧古斯丁．菲涅耳（Augustin Fresnel）的科學家推出一種新型透鏡，最早裝在法國的一座燈塔上。它不是一整塊厚玻璃，而是用數百個精心切割的稜鏡，把四散的光線折成一道強烈的光束。菲涅耳透鏡損失的光不超過 20%，最大型的透鏡在海上 20 多英里外都看得見。由於透鏡可以旋轉，每座燈塔還能閃出自己獨特的閃光模式，讓水手分辨不同的燈塔。

這些更亮的燈仍然要靠人。守塔人日落時點燈、日出時熄燈，夜裡爬上塔頂替轉動透鏡的發條機械上發條，還要花好幾個小時擦亮玻璃。他們的工作之一是修剪燃燒中的燈芯，以免冒煙弄髒透鏡，因此得到「wickies」（燈芯人）這個綽號。

電力開始改變這一切。美國的燈塔在 1900 年開始改用電力，起初進展很慢，到了 1920、1930 年代則迅速普及。要做的工作變少了，需要的守塔人也跟著減少；1960 年代中期，美國開始推動燈塔自動化的計畫。到了 1990 年，除了波士頓燈塔（Boston Light）之外，美國每一座燈塔都已不再有守塔人。如今，GPS 讓燈塔遠不如從前重要，許多老燈塔改成博物館，甚至成了可以過夜的住宿地點。

details.method_zh: 逐句比對選文、題幹與選項中的事實與數字和事實單；第 1 輪退回的句子（f19）與新改的解析重新開啟 NPS「History of Lighthouses in the United States」、NPS Cape Hatteras「The Fresnel Lens」原文確認；其餘未變更的句子沿用第 1 輪對 NPS、National Geographic 原文的逐條核對。文中沒有事實單以外的具體細節。
